one_liner: A wide-moat business worth owning, but it trades at 2.0x fair value. Interesting below about $54.

profile.what: BNY (formerly Bank of New York Mellon) is the world's largest custodian bank, holding and servicing over $50 trillion of assets for pension funds, asset managers and governments. It also runs the Pershing brokerage platform.
profile.money: Fees for safekeeping assets, settling trades, clearing, payments and fund administration, plus net interest income on client deposits. Fees rise with market values and transaction volumes.
profile.valued: BNY is valued on P/E and price to tangible book. The multiple has risen as returns improved under a cost and growth programme; it is more stable than other banks because it does little lending.
profile.peer_group: Financials · bank, insurer or asset manager

summary.sentence: The largest custodian bank: steady fees, little lending risk.
strengths: Fee-based and less credit-sensitive than lending banks.
risks: Priced at over twice book value.
Earnings benefit from high interest rates.

meaning.what_it_does: The world's largest custody bank, safekeeping and servicing assets for institutions.
meaning.how_it_makes_money: Fees for custody, clearing and asset servicing, plus interest on deposits.
meaning.how_it_keeps_making_money: Institutions rarely move trillions of dollars of assets between custodians.
meaning.how_it_could_stop: Fee pressure, or an operational failure.

moat.summary: One of a handful of custodians large enough to serve global institutions.

industry.summary: Custody is plumbing: essential and slow to change.

management.summary: Margins and returns have improved markedly.

valuation.method: Banks are valued on book value, not free cash flow. Justified price-to-book = (ROE − 3% growth) ÷ (required return − 3%), using a normalised ROE of 11.1% (median of the last three fiscal years and TTM, capped at 25%) and a required return of 11% (low) to 9% (high): 1.01–1.35 × book value per share of $65.58.

methods.name: Excess-return model on book value
methods.basis: Book value per share $65.58 × 1.01–1.35. This is how Damodaran values banks and insurers: equity is worth book value plus the returns earned above the cost of equity.
